length.text: Usually up to 1.6 m; large males just over 2 m

overview.text: The Aesculapian Snake is one of Europe's largest snakes and an excellent climber. It is named after Asclepius (Aesculapius), the Greek and Roman god of medicine: the snake coiled around his staff, still used in medical logos today, is thought to be this species.

identification.text: Adults are light brown to bronze with smooth scales that give a metallic sheen, sometimes with small white dots. The belly scales are angled sharply at the sides, which helps it climb.

size.label: Adults
size.text: Usually not longer than about 1.6 m; males grow larger than females and may reach just over 2 m.

variation.label: Young
variation.text: Juveniles are light green or brownish-green with darker markings along the back and sides.

variation.label: Sexes
variation.text: Adult males grow larger than females.

distribution.label: Native
distribution.text: From eastern France across central and southern Europe to the Balkans and the Black Sea region, and south into northern Italy. A closely related Italian form has been raised to a separate species, the Italian Aesculapian Snake (*Zamenis lineatus*).

distribution.label: Introduced
distribution.text: Small introduced populations exist in Britain.

habitat.text: Warm, moderately humid, hilly or rocky forested places; it avoids open plains and intensively farmed land.

behaviour.text: A good climber, often seen in bushes and trees, where it raids bird nests.

diet.text: Mainly small mammals - shrews, moles and rodents up to the size of rats - plus birds, their eggs and nestlings.

funfacts.text: The snake on the medical symbol, the Rod of Asclepius, is believed to be an Aesculapian Snake.
